summary: Defines the PPP Internet Protocol Control Protocol, which sets up and configures IP over a PPP link. After PPP's link is up, IPCP negotiates the IP settings for the two ends.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Protocol Control Protocol (IPCP) is the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) negotiation that configures Internet Protocol on a link. The peers agree on addresses and whether to shorten Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) headers before sending IP packets.

subtitle: How PPP links negotiate IP addresses and optional TCP/IP header compression.

tldr.problem: After a point-to-point link is established, its two ends still need to configure which network-layer protocol to carry and which IP addresses to use.
tldr.mechanism: IPCP reuses PPP's configuration exchange to negotiate IP settings and optional Van Jacobson TCP/IP header compression.
tldr.outcome: When IPCP reaches the Opened state, IP packets can cross the link. RFC 1332 obsoletes RFC 1172 and was later updated by RFC 3241.

sections.title: Where IPCP Fits in PPP
sections.content:
Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) has a Link Control Protocol (LCP) to establish and test a link, plus Network Control Protocols (NCPs) to configure network-layer protocols. RFC 1332 defines the IP Control Protocol (IPCP), the NCP for Internet Protocol.

PPP first configures the data link using LCP. It then configures IP using IPCP; only after that protocol reaches its Opened state can IP packets be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP first checks and configures the link, then configures the network protocol that will use it. IPCP performs that second step for IP.

sections.title: How IPCP Exchanges Configuration
sections.content:
IPCP uses the same packet-exchange mechanism as LCP. One IPCP packet is carried in a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hexadecimal 8021. IPCP uses Codes 1 through 7 for configuration, termination, and code rejection.

IPCP packets are exchanged only after PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase. An implementation should allow authentication and link-quality checks to finish before timing out while waiting for a response.
sections.plainLanguage: IPCP asks and answers configuration questions using the exchange mechanism PPP already uses for the link. It waits until the link is ready before negotiating IP.

sections.title: Sending IP Datagrams
sections.content:
IP packets can be sent only after PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase and IPCP reaches Opened. Each IP packet is placed in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hexadecimal 0021.

The largest IP packet is limited by the largest Information field supported by the PPP link. Larger datagrams must be fragmented if they are sent across the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Once negotiation is complete, each IP packet travels in a PPP frame. A packet larger than the link's information field must be split into fragments.

sections.title: Negotiating IP Addresses
sections.content:
The IP-Address option lets a peer request a particular local IP address or use four zero octets to ask the other peer to provide one. The peer can return a valid address in a Configure-Nak. By default, IPCP assigns no IP address.

The older IP-Addresses option is deprecated because negotiation may not converge in every case. IP-Address replaces it and is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Each peer can request an address or ask the other peer to provide one. The RFC prefers the IP-Address option over the older IP-Addresses option.

sections.title: Negotiating Header Compression
sections.content:
The IP-Compression-Protocol option negotiates whether a specific compression protocol can be received. Compression is off by default. For Van Jacobson compressed TCP/IP, the protocol value is hexadecimal 002d.

Van Jacobson compression reduces TCP/IP headers to as few as 3 bytes. Each end must request the option separately to receive compressed packets in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers can separately agree to receive compressed TCP/IP headers. This can reduce a header to as few as 3 bytes, which the RFC says can help on slow serial lines.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed in this memo. Its appendix recommends the IP-Compression-Protocol option with at least 4 slots, usually 16, and IP-Address only on dial-up lines.

RFC 1332 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1172 and was updated by RFC 3241. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes RFC 1332.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not discuss security issues. RFC 3241 later updated this Proposed Standard, which replaced RFC 1172.

fields.name: IP-Address
fields.desc: Four octets for the requested local address; all zero requests an address from the peer.
